demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette: Eleanor sits across from me, her hands folded tightly in her lap. The afternoon light catches the silver in her hair, but her posture remains rigid, as if bracing for a door to swing open. When she describes the night three years ago, her breathing shifts. The call comes at 2 a.m. A police officer's voice tells her that her thirty-four-year-old son, Leo, has been struck by a drunk driver on the interstate. The words do not make sense at first. She sits on the edge of the bed, waiting for him to walk through the door laughing. When she finally understands, the room tilts. She drives to the hospital with hands white on the wheel, her breath coming in short, sharp gasps that feel like glass in her throat. She arrives just as the machinery stops. In the months that follow, her house fills with a silence so thick she learns to walk on the balls of her feet. She thinks constantly of her forty years managing a regional library, where she once cataloged chaos into order. Now, she cannot bear to look at the wooden boxes still stacked in the basement. Every time she passes them, her chest contracts, and she sees the exact shade of gray in Leo's jacket-the one he wears that night. She stops breathing. Her mind races, rewinding the radio broadcast she still keeps on her phone, replaying the weather report, the traffic updates, the final seconds before impact. She checks her own heartbeat when her phone vibrates. When her husband, Robert, tries to hold her, she flinches, her muscles locking before she consciously remembers who stands beside her. She apologizes afterward, but the reflex does not care. At sixty-eight, her retirement becomes a landscape of avoidance. She wakes at 4 a.m. every morning because her nervous system refuses to settle. She sits in the kitchen, watching streetlamps flicker off one by one, convinced the next siren will pull her back to that Tuesday night. She stops driving on highways. When Robert asks to take the car to visit his sister, she feels a hot wave of nausea and insists on walking, though her knees ache. She tells herself she wants fresh air, but steering wheels feel like traps. Her mind constantly scans for exits in every room. She rearranges the furniture twice last month because the living room layout suddenly feels too exposed. She cannot sleep more than two hours without waking to check the deadbolt, the window, then her phone, though she knows the screen is dark. Robert brings her coffee in the evenings, setting it down softly. She drinks it without tasting it, her attention fixed on the rhythm of her pulse in her ears. She remembers Leo's laugh so vividly it brings tears, but the joy curdles quickly into suffocating guilt. Why did she let him drive? Why didn't she answer his text from an hour earlier? These questions loop through her mind, each repetition tightening her shoulders until she has to stand up and pace the hallway. She stops attending book club. She tells friends she is tired, but their casual questions make her throat close. She smiles through it, nodding, while inside she rehearses the way out of the conversation. In this room, she unspools slowly. She talks about the weight of the silence at home, the way autumn leaves trigger a sudden, sharp dread when they fall too fast. She describes how she still sets two places at dinner now, automatically, before remembering. Her hands tremble when she reaches for her tea. She speaks of the nights when the house creaks and her body tenses until she recognizes it as just the pipes cooling. She does not describe this as a list of changes. She describes it as living inside a glass jar, watching the world continue normally while she waits for the next fracture. The years have not softened the edges of what happens; they have only taught her how to carry it quietly, hour by hour, breath by breath, while Robert wonders how to reach her.
